story: While Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance was crushed in the Weddell Sea, his Ross Sea party faced a desperate two-year ordeal on the opposite side of Antarctica. Believing Shackleton's transcontinental crossing was imminent, nine men hauled thousands of pounds of supplies across the treacherous Ross Ice Shelf to lay vital depots. Without a ship, proper gear, or communication, they improvised clothing from tent canvas and lived on seal meat. Despite battling blinding blizzards and severe scurvy, three men died before completing their mission in full. When Shackleton finally arrived to rescue them in January 1917, the survivors learned the horrifying truth: their agonizing toil and the deaths of their comrades had been entirely for nothing, as Shackleton never even reached the continent.
angle: The Ross Sea party spent two years dying of scurvy to lay supply depots for Shackleton, never knowing his ship had been crushed on the other side of the continent.

claims.claim: Ten men were left stranded ashore at Cape Evans after the Aurora drifted away.

evidence.quote: Ten men were left stranded ashore at Cape Evans.
10 men had not been aboard when the gale struck and so were marooned at Cape Evans on Antarctica, with only the clothes they were wearing, and a stack of supplies intended for Shackleton.

claims.claim: The stranded shore party improvised clothing and gear using supplies and material left behind by Scott's and Shackleton's earlier expeditions.

evidence.quote: Their first recourse was to the food and materials from supplies left behind by Scott's and Shackleton's earlier expeditions.
In the endless polar night, broken sledges and Primus stoves were cobbled together, tattered tents sewn into clothing, and finnesko sleeping bags fashioned into boots.

claims.claim: Following the rescue, Albert Medals were awarded to Ernest Joyce, Dick Richards, Ernest Wild, and Victor Hayward.

evidence.quote: On 4 July 1923, Joyce and Richards were awarded Albert Medals by George V for their bravery and life-saving efforts during the second depot-laying journey. Wild and Victor Hayward received the same award, posthumously.
Joyce, Wild, Hayward, and Richards later received the Albert Medal for their heroic devotion to duty.
